extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and critics of Spinoza, translators of philosophical works, students of Scripture interpretation and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical guidance and evaluative principles for interpreting the Bible and for assessing Spinoza's Treatise Theologico-Politicus, including advice for translators, criteria for prophetic revelation, textual/ canonical criticism, and the proper relation of theology and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's requirement: Latin familiarity or collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation of Spinoza requires accurate knowledge of Latin; a translator who manifests little familiarity with Latin should unite his forces with someone who has that accurate knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises the English translator to 'unite his forces with some one who has that accurate knowledge of Latin which he himself has not, and then, perhaps, of that union a really good translation of Spinoza will be the result.' An initial specimen of a translator's force may give the experienced reader an instinct to stop reading (smile or sigh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions indispensable for adequate interpretation of Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand any prophet thoroughly one ought to know the life, character, and pursuits of that prophet, under what circumstances his book was composed, and in what state and through what hands it has come down to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spinoza points out these are often unknowable now and hence a perfectly adequate interpretation may be impossible; still, the main sense of Scripture's books may be clearly seized despite these limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit assertions about prophecy to prophets' clear declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing should be asserted about prophecy except what is clearly declared by the prophets themselves, because prophecy is a revelation of which the laws of ordinary human nature cannot be the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since prophecy 'does not fall within the scope of our ordinary knowing faculties,' ignorant readers not versed in Hebrew genius and phraseology may misattribute to prophets assertions they do not clearly make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic revelation conveyed via words, images, and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural prophecy is represented as received through words and images; prophets excelled by vividness of representation and imagination rather than by perfection of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the frequent use of figures and the varied, sometimes improper, expressions about God (examples: Moses attributing passions to God; Micaiah's throne; Daniel's old-man imagery; disciples seeing the Spirit as a dove).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and moral certitude of true prophets
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential qualifications of a true prophet are the power of imagining, the power of feeling what goodness is, and the habit of practising goodness; prophets attained certainty by the testimony of a sign and, above all, by the testimony of their own conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even this yields only moral, not mathematical, certainty—no man can be perfectly sure of his own goodness. A bad prophet may present signs yet lack moral certitude, rendering his doctrine untrue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of religion: love of God and neighbour
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Old and New Testaments contain very few and very simple essentials: the precept to love God and our neighbour (e.g., Isaiah ch.1 precepts; Sermon on the Mount injunctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precepts identify the Bible as the Word of God despite its containing history and reasoning which may sometimes be false; they correspond to the universal divine law written in the heart and establish Scripture's divinity in a secondary sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish universal divine law from temporal human law
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine law (the method for attaining highest blessedness) is universal and written in the heart; human law is concerned with temporal security and is dictated by a lawgiver, varying by nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Jewish case the revealed law's fundamental precept (obey God and keep commandments) was framed with temporal aims (continuity of the State); Jewish election was temporal and limited to the duration of the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles should be interpreted in light of reason, language, and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason regards a miracle (a breach of the laws of nature) as impossible; Scripture nowhere asserts as a general truth that miracles are possible, and apparent miracles should be examined for natural explanations and the rhetorical tropes of Hebrew narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To know what Scripture means about each seeming miracle we must know tropes, Hebrew phrases, circumstances (e.g., Red Sea passage and the east wind), and the speaker's preconceived opinions; to suppose God violates natural law is to dishonour God, since laws of nature are laws of God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject literal/verbal inspiration; evaluate textual authorship and compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: The vulgar notion of verbal inspiration and absolute truth in every word/sentence is false; internal testimony shows many biblical books were compiled after Jerusalem's destruction by fallible compilers and contain extracts from conflicting sources, errors, and unsettled readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophetic books are often fragments collected by rabbis; Books of Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Daniel post-date Judas Maccabeus; the Canon was fixed by human councils—therefore one must not assume verbal infallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat all Scriptural parts as equipollent; weigh context and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents within Scripture are of unequal value and varying applicability; one must discriminate between different characters of texts and not use isolated expressions promiscuously as if of identical force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spinoza is criticized for sometimes quoting Ecclesiastes as equal to Moses or using Jeremiah to assert speculative ideas Jeremiah never held; one must consider whether an isolated text is annulled by context, general drift, or more authoritative passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain separate spheres for theology and philosophy; avoid doctrinal coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy has its sphere (perfect knowledge) and theology its sphere (perfect obedience); neither has the right to invade and subdue the other, and theology should demand only what is indispensable to obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative opinions beyond fundamentals should not be promulgated as essentials by governments or national churches; governments should concede the fullest liberty of speculation and avoid making metaphysical formularies the national creed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate speculative opinions by their practical effect on obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative opinions beyond fundamental religion are to be judged pious or impious according to whether they confirm or shake the believer in the practice of obedience, not simply by their truth or falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The truest speculative opinion is impious if it makes its holder rebellious; conversely, a false speculative opinion may be pious if it promotes obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture offers moral testimony enabling the salvation of the many
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture teaches that obedience without knowledge may lead to salvation; this testimony offers moral certainty important because only a small minority can live virtuously by reason alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief in this testimony is a comfort: without Scripture's testimony 'we should ... be in doubt respecting the salvation of nearly the whole human race.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical method consistency: declare hypotheses and reconcile contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic should state his own opinion about Scripture's fundamental character and be methodologically consistent—avoiding treating Scripture sometimes as literal and other times as critical without reconciling the two approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader is baffled when Spinoza, proceeding by hypothesis, accepts the 'vera vox' of Sinai as recorded yet elsewhere asserts a priori that miracles are impossible; a critic must reconcile how purportedly miraculous scriptural events can be treated within his declared method.
